title: No. 73 — The Provision For The Support of the Executive, and the Veto Power (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The third ingredient toward constituting the vigor of the executive authority is an adequate provision for its support. It is plain that without proper attention to this point, the separation of the executive from the legislative department would be merely nominal and meaningless. The legislature, with discretionary power over the salary and emoluments of the Chief Magistrate, could render him as obsequious to its will as it pleased. In most cases, it could either reduce him by hunger or tempt him by lavish gifts to surrender his judgment to its inclinations. These expressions, taken in their full breadth, would no doubt convey more than is intended. There are men who could be neither distressed nor seduced into sacrificing their duty. But this stern virtue grows in few soils. In the main, it will be found that power over a man's support is power over his will. If it were necessary to confirm so plain a truth by facts, examples would not be lacking, even in this country, of the intimidation or seduction of the Executive by the threats or allurements of the legislative body's pecuniary arrangements.

It is not easy, therefore, to commend too highly the judicious attention paid to this subject in the proposed Constitution. It provides that "The President of the United States shall, at stated times, receive for his services a compensation which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period for which he shall have been elected; and he shall not receive within that period any other emolument from the United States, or any of them." It is impossible to imagine any provision more eligible than this. The legislature, on the appointment of a President, is once and for all to declare what the compensation for his services shall be during the term for which he has been elected. Once this is done, it has no power to alter it, either by increase or diminution, until a new period of service begins by a new election. It can neither weaken his fortitude by acting on his needs, nor corrupt his integrity by appealing to his avarice. Neither the Union nor any of its members will be free to give, nor will he be free to receive, any other emolument than what was determined by the first act. He can thus have no pecuniary inducement to renounce or desert the independence the Constitution intended for him.
The last of the requirements for energy listed are competent powers. Let us proceed to consider those proposed to be vested in the President of the United States.

The first thing that strikes our notice is the President's qualified veto over the acts or resolutions of the two houses of the legislature. In other words, his power to return all bills with objections, with the effect of preventing them from becoming laws unless they are afterwards ratified by two-thirds of each house.

The tendency of the legislative department to intrude on the rights, and to absorb the powers, of the other departments has already been noted and repeated. The insufficiency of a mere parchment outline of the boundaries of each has also been remarked upon. The necessity of furnishing each with constitutional weapons for its own defense has been inferred and proved. From these clear and indisputable principles follows the propriety of a veto, either absolute or qualified, in the Executive over the acts of the legislative branches. Without one or the other, the Executive would be absolutely unable to defend himself against the encroachments of the legislature. He could be gradually stripped of his authorities by successive resolutions, or destroyed by a single vote. In one way or the other, the legislative and executive powers might quickly come to be combined in the same hands. Even if no tendency had ever shown itself in the legislative body to invade the rights of the Executive, the rules of just reasoning and theoretical propriety would themselves teach us that one ought not to be left to the mercy of the other, but ought to possess a constitutional and effective power of self-defense.

But the power in question has a further use. It serves not only as a shield to the Executive but also as an additional security against the enactment of improper laws. It establishes a beneficial check on the legislative body, designed to guard the community against the effects of faction, hastiness, or any impulse unfriendly to the public good that may happen to influence a majority of that body.

The propriety of a veto has on some occasions been opposed by the observation that we cannot presume one man would have more virtue and wisdom than a number of men, and that unless we make this presumption, it would be improper to give the executive magistrate any kind of control over the legislative body.

But this observation, when examined, will appear specious rather than solid. The propriety of the thing does not turn on supposing superior wisdom or virtue in the Executive, but on supposing that the legislature will not be infallible — that the love of power may sometimes betray it into a disposition to encroach on the rights of other branches of government; that a spirit of faction may sometimes pervert its deliberations; that impressions of the moment may sometimes hurry it into measures that, on more mature reflection, it would itself condemn. The chief inducement for conferring this power on the Executive is to enable him to defend himself; the secondary inducement is to increase the chances for the community against the passing of bad laws through haste, inadvertence, or design. The more often a measure is brought under examination, and the greater the diversity of situations among those examining it, the less the danger of errors flowing from lack of due deliberation, or of missteps coming from the contagion of a common passion or interest. It is far less probable that culpable views of any kind should infect every part of the government at the same moment, and concerning the same object, than that they should govern and mislead each in turn.

It may perhaps be said that the power to prevent bad laws also includes the power to prevent good ones, and may be used for one as well as the other. But this objection will carry little weight with those who can rightly estimate the harm of the inconstancy and instability of laws — which is the greatest blemish on the character and spirit of our governments. They will consider every institution designed to restrain the excess of lawmaking, and to keep things as they are at any given period, as much more likely to do good than harm. It is favorable to greater stability in the system of legislation. The injury possibly done by defeating a few good laws will be amply compensated by the advantage of preventing many bad ones.

Nor is this all. The superior weight and influence of the legislative body in a free government, and the risk to the Executive in a contest of strength with that body, provide a satisfactory security that the veto would generally be used with great caution. There would more often be room for a charge of timidity than of rashness in its use. A king of Great Britain, with all his train of sovereign attributes and all the influence he draws from a thousand sources, would today hesitate to veto the joint resolutions of the two houses of Parliament. He would not fail to exert the utmost of his influence to strangle a measure disagreeable to him on its way to the throne, to avoid the dilemma of either permitting it to take effect or risking the displeasure of the nation by opposing the sense of the legislative body. Nor is it likely that he would finally venture to exert his prerogatives except in a case of manifest propriety or extreme necessity. All well-informed men in that kingdom will agree to the justice of this remark. A very considerable period has passed since the crown's veto has been exercised.

If a magistrate so powerful and so well fortified as a British monarch would have qualms about exercising the power in question, how much greater caution may reasonably be expected in a President of the United States, clothed for the short period of four years with the executive authority of a government wholly and purely republican?

It is plain that there would be greater danger of his not using his power when necessary than of his using it too often, or too much. Indeed, an argument against its expediency has been drawn from this very source. It has been represented as a power odious in appearance and useless in practice. But it does not follow that because it might rarely be exercised, it would never be exercised. In the case for which it is chiefly designed — an immediate attack on the constitutional rights of the Executive, or one in which the public good was plainly and palpably sacrificed — a man of tolerable firmness would use his constitutional means of defense and would heed the admonitions of duty and responsibility. In the first case, his fortitude would be stimulated by his immediate interest in the power of his office; in the second, by the probable approval of his constituents, who, although they would naturally lean toward the legislative body in a doubtful case, would hardly let their partiality mislead them in a very plain one. I speak here of a magistrate with only an ordinary share of firmness. There are men who, under any circumstances, will have the courage to do their duty at every risk.

But the convention has pursued a middle course in this business, one that will both facilitate the exercise of the power vested in the executive magistrate and make its efficacy depend on the sense of a considerable part of the legislative body. Instead of an absolute veto, it is proposed to give the Executive the qualified veto already described. This is a power that would be much more readily exercised than the other. A man who might be afraid to defeat a law by his single VETO might not hesitate to return it for reconsideration, subject to being finally rejected only if more than one-third of each house concurred in the sufficiency of his objections. He would be encouraged by the thought that if his opposition prevailed, it would carry with it a very respectable portion of the legislative body, whose influence would join his in supporting the propriety of his conduct in the public eye. A direct and categorical veto has something in its appearance more harsh, and more apt to irritate, than the mere offering of argumentative objections to be approved or disapproved by those to whom they are addressed. To the extent it would be less apt to offend, it would be more apt to be exercised; and for this very reason, it may in practice prove more effective. It is to be hoped that it will not often happen that improper views will govern so large a proportion as two-thirds of both branches of the legislature at the same time — and this, too, in spite of the counterweight of the Executive. It is in any case far less probable that this should be the case than that such views should taint the resolutions and conduct of a bare majority. A power of this kind in the Executive will often have a silent and unnoticed, though forceful, effect. When men engaged in unjustifiable pursuits know that obstructions may come from a quarter they cannot control, they will often be restrained by the mere apprehension of opposition from doing what they would otherwise eagerly rush into.

This qualified veto, as remarked elsewhere, is in this state vested in a council consisting of the governor, with the chancellor and judges of the Supreme Court, or any two of them. It has been freely used on a variety of occasions, and frequently with success. Its utility has become so apparent that persons who, when the Constitution was being compiled, were violent opposers of it, have from experience become its declared admirers.(1)

I have remarked elsewhere that the convention, in framing this part of their plan, departed from the model of this state's constitution in favor of that of Massachusetts. Two strong reasons may be imagined for this preference. One is that the judges, who are to be the interpreters of the law, might receive an improper bias from having previously given an opinion in their revisionary capacity. The other is that by being often associated with the Executive, they might be drawn too far into the political views of that magistrate, so that a dangerous combination might gradually form between the executive and judiciary departments. It is impossible to keep the judges too distinct from every other occupation than that of expounding the laws. It is especially dangerous to put them in a position to be either corrupted or influenced by the Executive.
1. Mr. Abraham Yates, a warm opponent of the plan of the convention, is of this number.
